Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current Domain Adaptation (DA) systems largely rely on restrictive assumptions that limit their real-world applicability. Most existing methods assume a "closed-set" scenario where the source and target domains share the exact same label space. Furthermore, they often require access to raw source data during the adaptation phase.

In practical deployment, we face a far more complex environment:
1.  **Heterogeneity:** We have multiple source domains, but they do not share the same label space (varying label sets).
2.  **Open-Set Conditions:** The target domain contains novel, "unknown" classes that were never seen in any source domain.
3.  **Source-Free Constraints:** Due to privacy concerns (e.g., medical imaging) or storage limits, we often only have access to pre-trained source models, not the original source data.

There is currently no unified learning theory or framework that effectively addresses **Multi-Source Semi-Supervised Open-Set Domain Adaptation (MSODA)**, particularly when source data is absent and source models utilize different architectures.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can build a robust unified target model by establishing a theoretical bound on the target error via "joint error" minimization. By aligning all source domains with the limited labeled target data, we can implicitly learn to distinguish between "known" and "unknown" categories.

Furthermore, we posit that raw source data is unnecessary for this alignment. We believe we can **generate** synthetic, labeled source feature anchors solely by leveraging the knowledge encoded in pre-trained source models. By using an attention-based mechanism to reconstruct features, we can bridge the domain gap and align distributions without ever violating data privacy constraints.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a comprehensive framework designed to transfer knowledge from multiple heterogeneous source models to a target domain containing both known and unknown classes.

**1. Theoretical Foundation: Joint Error Minimization**
We will formulate a learning objective based on a "joint error" theory. Instead of aligning each source to the target independently, we will optimize a convex combination of errors. We will employ a log-sum-exp smoothing strategy to adaptively combine gradients from multiple sources, stabilizing the training process against domain shifts.

**2. Source-Free Feature Generation (The "Attention" Module)**
To handle the absence of source data, we will design an **Attention-based Feature Generation (AFG)** module.
*   **Knowledge Extraction:** We will treat pre-trained source classifiers (potentially Bayesian linear classifiers) as repositories of source feature statistics.
*   **Anchor Generation:** We will use an attention mechanism where target features act as queries and keys. This module will learn to reconstruct "source-like" labeled features (anchors) by projecting target data into the source feature space.
*   **Loss Constraints:** We will employ a reconstruction loss to ensure fidelity and a **cycle-consistency loss** to ensure that features generated from labeled and unlabeled target data remain semantically consistent.

**3. Positive-Unlabeled (PU) Learning for Open-Set Recognition**
To accurately identify "unknown" classes in the target domain, we will integrate Multi-class Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning.
*   We will treat the known classes as "Positive" and the rest of the target data as "Unlabeled."
*   This allows us to estimate the expected risk of the unknown class without requiring labeled negative samples.

**4. Progressive Unknown Rejection (PUR)**
Aligning the target distribution to source anchors is risky if the target data contains many "unknown" samples (outliers). We will implement a progressive filtering strategy.
*   During training, we will rank target samples based on their likelihood of belonging to the unknown class.
*   We will gradually increase a threshold to reject these high-likelihood unknown samples from the alignment process, ensuring that we only align "known" target samples with the generated source anchors.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Generalization:** We aim to provide a rigorous learning theory for Multi-Source Open-Set Domain Adaptation, offering error bounds that account for varying label spaces across domains.
*   **Privacy-Preserving Adaptation:** By introducing the Attention-based Feature Generation module, we enable domain adaptation without accessing raw source data, solving a critical bottleneck in privacy-sensitive applications.
*   **Architecture Agnostic:** Our approach allows the target model to have a completely different architecture (e.g., Vision Transformers) from the source models (e.g., ResNets), significantly increasing flexibility in deployment.
*   **Robust Open-Set Performance:** The integration of PU learning and progressive rejection is expected to significantly improve the model's ability to reject unknown classes while maintaining high accuracy on known categories.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed Unified Model (UM) and its source-free variant (UM+AFG) for Multi-Source Semi-supervised Open-set Domain Adaptation (MSODA).

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Office-Home:** Contains 15,500 images from 65 categories across 4 domains (Art, Clipart, Product, Real-World).
        *   *Class Split:* The first 30 classes (alphabetical order) were selected as "known" classes. The remaining classes were grouped as "unknown".
        *   *Source Configuration:* Each source domain contained 10 non-overlapping classes (large label shift).
    *   **DomainNet:** A large-scale dataset. We selected 4 domains (Real, Clipart, Painting, Sketch) comprising 126 classes.
        *   *Class Split:* The first 60 classes were selected as "known". The rest were grouped as "unknown".
        *   *Source Configuration:* Each source domain contained 20 non-overlapping classes.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **OS*:** Normalized accuracy for known classes only.
    *   **UNK:** Accuracy for the unknown class.
    *   **HOS:** Harmonic mean of OS* and UNK, defined as $2 \times (OS^* \times UNK) / (OS^* + UNK)$. This was the primary metric for overall performance.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   *Source-Combine / Multi-Source Methods:* OSBP, PGL, ANNA, PUJE, MOSDANET, HyMOS.
    *   *Source-Free Methods:* MPU, OSBP* (adapted), PUJE* (adapted), MOSDANET* (adapted). (Note: Existing methods were adapted for source-free settings using pseudo-source data as they cannot natively address open-set source-free tasks with label shift).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Backbones:** ResNet-50 (ImageNet pre-trained) was the primary backbone. ViT-B/16 was used to test architectural flexibility.
    *   **Optimization:** SGD with momentum 0.9.
    *   **Learning Rate:** Initial learning rate set to 0.001, used a learning rate annealing strategy.
    *   **Batch Size:** Fixed at 24.
    *   **Augmentation:** RandomFlip, RandomCrop, and RandAugment.
    *   **Hyperparameters:** 
        *   Trade-off parameter $\lambda$: 0.01.
        *   PU coefficient $\beta$: 0.15.
        *   Scaling coefficient $\nu$: 0.1.
        *   Threshold coefficient $\tau$: 0.3.
    *   **Setup:** We utilized a Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) for the adversarial alignment. For semi-supervised settings, we used 1-shot and 3-shot protocols (1 or 3 labeled samples per class).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Overall Performance:** We observed that UM consistently outperformed state-of-the-art results on both Office-Home and DomainNet. Specifically, we improved HOS by 3.6%/3.8% (1-shot/3-shot) on Office-Home and 6.1%/6.7% on DomainNet compared to baselines.
*   **Source-Free Performance:** The UM+AFG method significantly enhanced HOS scores in source-free settings, showing gains of 7.1%/7.0% in Office-Home and 4.9%/6.1% in DomainNet over comparable source-free baselines.
*   **Feature Alignment (t-SNE):** We visualized feature distributions for the Art task (Office-Home) and Real task (DomainNet). We observed that the proposed UM method achieved better alignment between source and target distributions compared to baselines (OSBP, HyMOS, PUJE, MOSDANET, PGL, ANNA). Specifically, the cluster of unknown target data (represented in green in visual outputs) showed a more discriminative class-wise decision boundary with UM.
*   **Robustness to Openness:** We varied the openness (ratio of unknown samples) in the target data $\{0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}$ for the Painting task. We observed that UM consistently outperformed baselines (PGL, PUJE*) across all openness levels. While PGL showed high variance, UM remained relatively stable.
*   **Convergence Stability:** We monitored recognition performance over training iterations for the Office-Home $\to$ Art task. We observed that while $OS^*$ experienced a slight downward trend, UNK accuracy kept improving. Crucially, UM reached a stable convergence, whereas some baselines failed to converge at the optimum or suffered severe performance drops in recognizing known classes.
*   **Impact of Sample Size:** We analyzed performance as the number of labeled target samples increased from 1 to 10 on DomainNet. We observed that UM maintained a lead over baselines. While cluster-based methods (OSBP, MOSDANET) were eventually caught by simple multi-class PU learning (MPU), UM consistently outperformed the competitive baseline PUJE. The source-free UM+AFG method's HOS score gradually approached and even surpassed methods using source data as sample size increased.
*   **Parameter Sensitivity:**
    *   **$\beta$ (PU Coefficient):** We observed that higher $\beta$ values generally led to more reliable unknown recognition performance, while the $OS^*$ score remained relatively stable.
    *   **$\nu$ (Scaling Factor):** We found that a larger $\nu$ focuses on the source domain contributing the most error. A smaller $\nu$ equalizes domain importance, which harmed performance when significant label shift existed (e.g., imbalanced label partitions).
    *   **$\tau$ (Threshold):** We observed a trade-off: a larger threshold $\tau$ led to higher UNK accuracy but at the cost of lower $OS^*$.
*   **Backbone Flexibility:** We verified that UM+AFG allows the target model to use a different backbone (ViT-B/16) than the source models (ResNet-50). Using ViT-B/16 provided a clear advantage, with HOS scores under source-free conditions approaching or outperforming source-data results using ResNet-50.
*   **Ablation Findings:** 
    *   $L_{sim}$ slightly improved the accuracy of the unknown class.
    *   Progressive Unknown Rejection (PUR) was found to be crucial; removing it caused a massive drop in UNK accuracy (e.g., from 73.7 to 39.6 on Office-Home).
    *   Cycle-consistency regularization ($L_{cyc}$) helped maintain the normalized accuracy of known classes.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
```

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Current Domain Adaptation (DA) paradigms generally assume a restricted "closed-set" scenario where source and target domains share an identical label space. However, real-world deployment often involves **Multi-Source Semi-Supervised Open-Set Domain Adaptation (MSODA)**. In this setting, we face three compounded challenges:
1.  **Heterogeneous Sources:** Labeled data originates from multiple source domains that do not share the same label space (varying label spaces).
2.  **Open-Set Targets:** The target domain contains novel "unknown" classes not present in the sources, causing negative transfer if forced into known categories.
3.  **Source-Free Constraints:** Due to privacy regulations or bandwidth limitations, we may not have access to original source data during adaptation, only pre-trained source models (which may differ in architecture).

Existing methods typically resort to naive source combination or fail to align distributions when the label spaces are disjoint. We define the problem as classifying unlabeled target data into either one of the known categories (union of source labels) or a common unknown class, utilizing only pre-trained source models and a few-shot labeled target set.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose a **Unified Model (UM)** grounded in a new learning theory based on **Joint Error**. We hypothesize that by minimizing a tighter upper bound of the target error—derived via a convex combination of source errors and discrepancies—we can effectively align heterogeneous domains.

To address the open-set and source-free constraints, we propose two specific mechanisms:
1.  **PU Learning for Expectation Estimation:** We will utilize Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning principles to estimate source domain expectations using only the "known" subset of the target domain, thereby bridging the label-space mismatch.
2.  **Attention-based Feature Generation (AFG):** We hypothesize that we can recover "source-like" features without accessing source data by learning an attention mechanism. This module will generate labeled anchors as a weighted average of target features, guided by the knowledge preserved in pre-trained Bayesian linear classifiers of the source models.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Mathematical Formulation of the MSODA Task
We define $N$ source domains $S_i'$ with varying label spaces. We have access to $n_i$ labeled points $\{(x_{s_i}^j, y_{s_i}^j)\}_{j=1}^{n_i}$ (or pre-trained models in the source-free case). We also possess a small set of labeled target points $V'$ (few-shot) and a large set of unlabeled target points $T$. The total output space is $\mathcal{V} = \{1, ..., K\}$, where $K$ represents the unknown class.

We seek a hypothesis $h: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{K}$ (outputting a probability vector) that minimizes the expected target error $\epsilon_T(h)$.

### 2. Target Error Bound via Joint Error
We will optimize the model based on a theoretical bound. Let $\epsilon_D(h, f^*)$ denote the expected disagreement between hypothesis $h$ and the true labeling function $f^*$ over distribution $D$. The target error is bounded by a convex combination of errors from multiple sources.

We formulate the empirical objective function using the **log-sum-exp trick** to smooth the optimization of the convex combination weights $\alpha_i$. We will minimize the following upper bound:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{total} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ L_{cls}^V(h) + \frac{1}{\nu} \log \sum_{i=1}^{N} \exp (\nu \hat{U}_i(h)) \right]
$$

Where:
*   $\nu > 0$ is a scaling coefficient.
*   $L_{cls}^V(h)$ is the classification error on the labeled target set.
*   $\hat{U}_i(h)$ represents the joint error contribution from source $i$, defined as:
    $$ \hat{U}_i(h) = L_{cls}^{S_i}(h) + 2 L_{dis}^i(f_{S_i}^*, f_V^*, f_T^*, h) $$
    Here, $L_{cls}^{S_i}$ is the source classification error, and $L_{dis}^i$ measures the discrepancy between the approximated true labeling functions ($f_{S_i}^*, f_V^*, f_T^*$) and the hypothesis $h$.

### 3. Inference on Expectation with PU Learning
Since source domains $S_i$ may lack the unknown class $K$ present in the target $T$, we cannot directly calculate discrepancies. We will employ PU learning to estimate the error on the complete source domain $S_i$ using the incomplete source domain $S_i^{\setminus K}$ (excluding unknown class) and the target domain.

We define the **Unknown Predictive Discrepancy** $v_D(h)$ as:
$$ v_D(h) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim D} | \log(1 - h(x)[K]) - \log(1 - e^K(x)[K]) | $$
where $e^K$ predicts inputs as the unknown class.

Using a class prior $\alpha$, we estimate the source error $\epsilon_{S_i}$ as:
$$ \epsilon_{S_i}(h \circ g) = \alpha [ \epsilon_{S_i^{\setminus K}}(h \circ g) - v_{S_i^{\setminus K}}(h \circ g) ] + v_T(h \circ g) $$
This formulation allows us to align features even when the source label space is a subset of the target label space.

### 4. Source-Free Knowledge Transfer: Attention-based Feature Generation (AFG)
In the source-free setting, we do not have $x_{s_i}$. We will utilize pre-trained source models comprising a feature extractor $g_i$ and a **Bayesian linear classifier** $f_i = \{\mu_i, \sigma_i\}$.

We will generate surrogate source features (anchors) $g(\hat{S}_i')$ by utilizing the unlabeled target features $\hat{T}'$. We introduce an attention module with query mapping $w_{q_i}$ and key mapping $w_{k_i}$. The generated source features are defined as:

$$ g(\hat{S}_i') = \text{softmax} \left( \frac{w_{q_i}(g_i(\hat{S}_i')) \cdot w_{k_i}(g_i(\hat{T}'))^\top}{\sqrt{F_i'}} \right) g(\hat{T}') $$

Here, $g_i(\hat{S}_i')$ represents sampled weights from the source Bayesian classifier using the re-parameterization trick: $\mu_i + \sigma_i \odot \zeta_i$ where $\zeta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$.

To train the mapping functions $w_{q_i}$ and $w_{k_i}$, we will minimize two losses:
1.  **Reconstruction Loss ($L_{rec}^i$):** Ensuring the attention module can reconstruct target features.
    $$ L_{rec}^i = \left| \text{softmax} \left( \frac{w_{q_i}(g_i(\hat{T}')) \cdot w_{k_i}(g_i(\hat{T}'))^\top}{\sqrt{F_i'}} \right) g(\hat{T}') - g(\hat{T}') \right| $$
2.  **Cycle-Consistency Loss ($L_{cyc}^i$):** Ensuring consistency between generated labeled features and labeled target features $\hat{V}'$.
    $$ L_{cyc}^i = \left| \text{softmax} \left( \frac{w_{q_i}(g_i(\hat{S}_i')) \cdot w_{k_i}(g_i(\hat{V}'))^\top}{\sqrt{F_i'}} \right) g(\hat{V}') - g(\hat{S}_i') \right| $$

### 5. Progressive Unknown Rejection (PUR)
To prevent the generated anchors from being contaminated by unknown class features present in the target data $\hat{T}$, we will implement a **Progressive Unknown Rejection** strategy.
We will define a threshold $\tau$ that increases according to an exponential ramp-up function. At each iteration, we rank target samples based on their predicted unknown probability $p(y=K|x_t)$. We effectively filter $\hat{T}$ to create $\hat{T}'$ by selecting the bottom $1-\tau$ samples (those least likely to be unknown) for the feature generation process.

### 6. Optimization and Architecture
*   **Feature Extractor ($g$):** We will use standard backbones (e.g., ResNet-50, ViT).
*   **Adversarial Alignment:** We will use a Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) to optimize the discrepancy term $L_{dis}$.
*   **Algorithm:**
    1.  Estimate known class ratio.
    2.  (If Source-Free): Update AFG weights $w$ and generate anchors $g(\hat{S}_i')$.
    3.  Compute errors $L_{cls}^V, L_{cls}^{S_i}$ and hypothesis constraints.
    4.  Compute discrepancy $L_{dis}^i$.
    5.  Update model parameters $\phi$ to minimize the log-sum-exp target error bound.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Theoretical Advancement:** We will provide a learning theory for Multi-Source Semi-Supervised Open-Set Domain Adaptation (MSODA) that explicitly bounds the generalization error in the presence of varying label spaces using a Joint Error approach.
2.  **Algorithmic Innovation:** The proposed Attention-based Feature Generation (AFG) will enable effective source-free adaptation that is computationally efficient and flexible regarding network architecture (allowing knowledge transfer between different backbones).
3.  **Robustness:** By integrating PU learning and Progressive Unknown Rejection, the framework will theoretically guarantee better separation of known and unknown classes, reducing the open-set risk inherent in real-world adaptation tasks.

network.web_access: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
